newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-CZECH CBANK MOVE EASING FAILS TO WEAKEN CZK.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CZECH CBANK MOVE EASING FAILS TO WEAKEN CZK.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) further eased its grip on the crown on Tuesday, and while it withstood initial predictions of weakening, analysts said any changes in rates could trigger another attack on the currency.

The CNB said that it had agreed with local large banks to renew access of non-residents to the Czech money market, which had been suspended on May 22, effectively freeing up crowns to the same speculators that had pushed it to record lows in May.

Analysts said that while the move was another positive sign for the market, it would have little effect on the crown since it was not coupled with an easing of interest rates which are keeping the crown strong.
"Well everyone expected this move. I think as soon as interest rates come down, which they soon will, the crown will go lower," Petr Kukla of Girocredit Bank told Reuters.
In late afternoon activity the crown was trading at about 18.524 against the mark just after the announcement, compared with 18.570 at the central bank's daily fixing at midday.

The CNB limited non-resident access to the local money market last month, as part of a series of measures aimed at easing downward pressure on the crown after a wave of short-selling pushed the currency to record lows.
"Individual banks will monitor crown loans to foreign clients, and these results will be directly at the dispostion of the CNB," a CNB statement said.
During the crown crisis, the CNB also raised its discount rate to 13 percent from a previous 10.5 percent, and the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent.

Eventually it cut off access to the Lombard facility as well as reaching an agreement with some local banks on cutting off non-resident access to the local money market to restrain availability of crowns.

"Immediately after the announcement, we saw some players try to push the crown lower but it seems that now the main feeling on the market is that there is selling pressure on foreign currency," said Breta Tichanek of ING bank.
"I think that for the time being, the crown will remain strong," he added.
The downward pressure eventually forced the CNB to allow the crown to float freely on May 27.
On Friday, the CNB said it would once again begin allowing banks access to the short-term last resort Lombard lending facility at the 50 percent rate.

The CNB has also loosened its tight grip on market liquidity in recent days through an easing of its reverse repo rate, which has fallen from 75 percent to 31 percent. Before the crown crisis, the central bank reverse repo rate stood at 12.4 percent.
